approved: Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2021
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would update Australia's rules on shipping hazardous waste abroad and into the country.
It would adopt standard enforcement powers from another Commonwealth law and create new offences and penalties for breaking the rules.
The bill would abolish a technical advisory group and instead require the minister to seek advice from suitable experts.
Meet Australia's international duties on plastic waste under the Basel Convention.
Adopt standard regulatory powers from the Regulatory Powers (Standard Provisions) Act 2014.
Introduce new strict liability offences, civil penalties, and aggravated offences for harming people or the environment.
Allow information sharing between Commonwealth, state, and territory governments.
Impose recordkeeping, information-gathering, and audit requirements.
Replace the Hazardous Waste Technical Group with a duty to consult appropriate experts.
Companies and individuals who export, import, or transit hazardous waste, and Commonwealth, state, and territory government agencies.

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2021-06-24.25.2) to the usual [second reading motion](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/), which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). This means that the amendment failed. ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House notes that after eight years this Government has yet to deliver any reforms to Australia's waste sector that have resulted in clear improvement to the health of our environment or significant progress towards a circular economy".*

The member moved an amendment to note that after eight years the government has failed to deliver any waste sector reforms that improved the environment or progressed a circular economy; while supporting the bill as a necessary update to implement Basel Convention changes on plastic waste, the member criticised the government for slow action, inadequate infrastructure, lack of end markets for recycled materials, and failure to meet its own 2025 recycling targets.

The speaker supported the Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2021, arguing that every nation should manage its own waste. They noted that about eight million tonnes of plastic enter the world’s oceans annually, with 99% sinking, and raised concerns about the cost and environmental impact of transporting regional waste long distances to landfill sites.

The member supported the amendment to the Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2021, arguing that government oversight and departmental resourcing are inadequate to enforce hazardous waste regulations, citing mangrove dieback at St Kilda in South Australia from saline brine discharge and insufficient monitoring of the Great Barrier Reef.

Katie Allen (Higgins) supported the Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2021, stating it fulfils Australia's Basel Convention obligations by strengthening controls on unsorted and hazardous plastic waste, introducing new penalties and replacing the Hazardous Waste Technical Group with a flexible mandatory consultation mechanism. She noted Australians generate 103 kilograms of plastic waste per person annually with only 12 per cent recycled, and that export bans on unprocessed plastics begin in July 2021 and July 2022.

The government argued the Hazardous Waste (Regulation of Exports and Imports) Amendment Bill 2021 aligns Australian laws with international Basel Convention obligations to better regulate hazardous waste movement. The speaker highlighted the Recycling Modernisation Fund, a $690 million federal commitment matched by industry and states, expected to create 10,000 jobs over 10 years, and emphasised turning waste into an economic opportunity.
